title: Robert Anton Wilson, High Weirdness, and Buddhist Meditation, with Erik Davis

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for modern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, emptiness, post-nondual and un-Buddhism, hardcore dharma, the unbearable beauty of existence, and more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast. And in this episode, I'm delighted to be speaking with the one and only Erik Davis. Erik Davis is an author, podcaster, award-winning journalist, and popular speaker based in San Francisco. He is probably best known for his book called TechGnosis: Myth, Magic, and Mysticism in the Age of Information, which is a cult classic of visionary media studies that investigates how our fascination with technology intersects with the religious imagination. It's a great book. You should check it out. And I also really love his podcast entitled Expanding Mind. Erik and I share a lot of obsessions in common, including meditation and the works of author Robert Anton Wilson. Erik and I recently met in a studio in San Francisco and created the episode that I called Robert Anton Wilson, High Weirdness, and Buddhist Meditation, with Erik Davis.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Erik, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Good to be here.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it's been quite a journey getting you here into the studio in the business district of San Francisco, but I'm glad you made it today.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: No, me too.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. So, you know, there's a lot going on. There's a lot I want to talk to you about. But the first thing is our mutual love for Robert Anton Wilson. You may not know this, but Robert Anton Wilson literally changed my life with his book Cosmic Trigger, which, just at the time I read it in the early 80s, was some kind of printed psychedelic pre-internet mind explosion that just literally rocketed me. Not literally, but it blew my mind and changed my life. And because I ended up working at Sounds True and could get interviews with various people I was interested in back then, I pulled strings and did a week-long interview with Robert Anton Wilson at his house in Santa Cruz in about '99, so not that long before he passed away. So it's been a lifelong fascination of mine, and I understand you're doing a book about him right now?

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Well, two chapters of the book that's coming out in the spring are devoted to him. It's called High Weirdness: Drugs, Visions, and Esoterica in the Seventies. And it's probably about the 70s as kind of a phase, a later phase of the counterculture, a different period of a certain kind of post-psychedelic or psychedelic searching, seeking — more occultism, more kind of existentialism, more darkness in a lot of ways than what the 60s were about in our imaginations. And then I focus it on the kinds of visionary experiences, the peak experiences, that create the high weirdness, with three figures: with Terence McKenna in the jungle, with the experiment at La Chorrera; Robert Anton Wilson with Cosmic Trigger; and Philip K. Dick with the 2-3-74 material, which is less psychedelic. But I kind of intentionally put those things together, because I think there's a tendency, when psychedelics are involved, to simply bracket it as psychedelics, and that's just what it's about, that's what tradition it belongs to. And while that makes sense for some reason, in other ways I think it's important to look at a broader range of kinds of experiences which can take similar forms.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And I think with Philip Dick — he had done acid and mescaline, but only a handful of times in his whole life, and he was years away from those experiences when he had his crazy stuff in 1974. But at the same time, it's very resonant. It's dissimilar, let's say, from elements of both Wilson's and McKenna's experiences. So I'm kind of interested in comparing them. But also, especially with Wilson — as my book is partly based on my PhD, so it's real scholarship, although it's written in a funny way, or an engaging way, hopefully — there's very little attention to Wilson outside of the narrow undergrounds that were influenced and even transformed by him. So unlike Phil Dick, where there's a whole scholarship around Phil Dick — McKenna less so, but he's kind of more of an outlier and in a lot of ways harder to wrap your head around. And while he was an intellectual, he doesn't have the cognitive intensity and singularity that Wilson does. He is going to blow your mind, and it's going to work like philosophy, except it's like philosophy you can't avoid, and it reprograms your way of thinking.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And I had a similar experience to you. I guess it was 1985, and I was living in Berkeley for the summer. I had just started to attend Yale, but my girlfriend at the time was in Berkeley, so I went back to Berkeley, and we were living in Barrington Hall, which is a legendary student co-op that at that point was still riding the kind of nadir of the counterculture. It was, you know, filled with junkies and crazy anarchists and occultists and drug dealers, cat piss and bong water, and there were murals and this sort of degraded haze of the counterculture. But it was still a really marvelous and esoteric, arcane place to live. And it was during that summer that I started to read Crowley and Wilson, reading Illuminatus! and Cosmic Trigger, and getting my mind suitably blown.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It was fascinating, because Illuminatus! was fun and I loved it. And of course Crowley still is a fascinating read even today, for me. Cosmic Trigger is different, though. It's like I can barely stand to read a page of it right now, even though I still really like Robert Anton Wilson's work and his writing. There's something about it — it was so of the moment. And I think it prefigures a lot of things about the internet and about modern culture in a very prescient way. And yet it's sort of a weird artifact that doesn't work anymore.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: I think the same could be said of Illuminatus! as well. I think Illuminatus! is, if anything, even a little bit more dated. But these things are hard to disentangle from their context, and that's sort of why the book that I decided to write is historical. It's like, something happened in the 70s — lots of things happened in the 70s. What do these crazy experiences of these outlier, eccentric intellectuals tell us about these larger forces that are going on at that time? Because I think you can't just pluck him out and say, oh, he's a good philosopher, oh, he's going to help you illuminate your life. There's something about a kind of transmission of an arcane, esoteric, druggie, hedonistic worldview or set of practices that there's no way could sustain and don't really make sense today in those terms. I mean, there's different forms of them today, but I think there is something really historically located about those things.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And yet, even if you set up the history and kind of understand it as an artifact of a certain era, there's a viral quality to that stuff. And I think part of that reaction is also like, I don't know if I want to get this dose again. You know, I think I got that one already, and it can scramble your perspectives. And that's a fun thing. That's true, I think, of all of these experiences as well, and the texts that came out of them. There's a certain memetic, infectious kind of quality to the questioning, to the style, the kind of mischievous playfulness combined with a kind of dark possibility, combined with a kind of existential, you're-on-your-own kind of aspect. I mean, it's really good for adolescence, man. It's like, you know, if you're young...

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I still say people should read Cosmic Trigger. I always thought it was possibly the most aptly named book in the world. At least for me, it really had that effect of just triggering a whole avalanche of psychedelic use and interest in meditation and so on. And it really did function in that way. I'm so impressed with his ability to almost see into the future, where now the way he was working is the way the entire cutting edge of the internet works. Unfortunately, it's now the alt-right using the same tricks that he was using to be mischievous, anarchist or whatever he was — whatever words you want to use for him, libertarian — so maybe even setting up some of today's craziness.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Oh, there's a whole conversation to be had there. I mean, one of the interesting things about doing this work, where I was particularly interested in going back to the late 50s and 60s and really trying to understand where he came from, so that I could create a kind of intellectual biography of where he was in the mid-70s when the Cosmic Trigger stuff happens. So, you know, he talks a lot about aspects of that story, but there are other things you can learn by reading his early columns in The Realist, for example. All that stuff's online, so you can go read all the articles he wrote for The Realist starting in the late 1950s, and you get a better sense of where his politics are coming from, which changed along the way.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: But it is really significant that he is not — as I would have to say neither McKenna nor Dick were — kind of men of the left. They weren't of exactly that particular articulation of the countercultural politics that we think of today as being not only dominant, but kind of exclusive. Especially McKenna was also more of an anarchist, more interested in technology and the way that technology was going to develop possibilities that could be liberational, as opposed to the kind of standard Luddite approach that you found either among hippies or among New Left people who were fearful or resistant to the power that was embodied in modern technology and computers or computer networks or things like that. And whereas these guys were like, oh no, let's see, let's see.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And so, I mean, Wilson's politics end up being complicated, because he is both a libertarian and an anarchist — and even the relationship between those two things we could sit here and talk for hours about. He even has a line from the early 70s, I think it's in Sex and Drugs, where he talks about representing a form of right-wing anarchism that is so radical it's more radical than left-wing. And so when he says right-wing, what does that mean in contemporary times? It doesn't really mean what we mean. What it means is radically individualist, as opposed to collectivist. And that's always been a tension in the countercultures. You have, on the one hand, communism and new forms of social movements and a very strong attention to collectivity, to comrades, even in communes, where it's very much about the collective. And then there's this other stream that's very individualistic, very socially libertarian, very much like, let's just see what happens, but I'm not going to follow your story, man. I'm not stuck in your... very, very individualistic. Don't tell me what to do.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, don't tell me what to do.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And he was much more of that style. So in some ways, technically, he's not unlike more modern forms of libertarianism, although even there we've got to say there's a difference between the libertarians of the 1990s and the libertarians of today by a considerable margin.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, quite a bit.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Quite a bit. But even that earlier phase — the thing that saves him, even if some of his ideas go in that kind of direction, is that, A, he always distrusted corporations. He was not a Hayek, you know, market-knows-all kind of guy. He did not believe that capitalism, taking the form of large corporations that were able to do whatever they want to do without state regulation, was the perfect model of a liberated society. He thought that was bullshit. And he came from a poor background, and he always had sympathy for poor people. He lived poor much of his life. He did use welfare at times. So he didn't have that hatred of the poor. And he thought a lot of libertarian positions were actually just hatred of the poor. So he had this kind of social sensibility that gave him an empathy and a different way of organizing his kind of anarchism. So it's much more palatable than a lot of the libertarian perspectives that we see today.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, I mean, he's raised a poor Irish kid on Long Island. He constantly, really deeply, has like Voltaire-level sympathy for the working class, regular people. It was always there in everything he wrote. I never saw a hint of anything but that, and I really respected that about him. You could tell there was a tremendous amount of kindness there and just personal ethos, right? He really had a practice of compassion, basically, or at least an experience of compassion.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So his anarchism also really goes into the core of, if you want to call it, his atheology, or the kind of spirituality, or mys— none of those words are really exactly right, but his cosmic view. And that was always very much against power, or against concentrated power, against institutionalized power. And that's, I think, one of the distinctions you can make: that a lot of contemporary libertarians think that the state is just kind of some sort of ossified nanny that is preventing them from doing whatever they want to do, or letting capital do what capital wants to do, or letting technology do what technology wants to do. But they're not really aware of the way that new oppressive forms of power emerge from these kinds of unleashed markets. Whereas if your libertarianism, or your anarchism, however you want to put it, is with a great suspicion of power at its core, then you move in a very different direction.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So for him there's a great kind of mythology story — I think Simon Moon describes it in Illuminatus! — where you go back and it's really about the emergence of the state and how the myths that you find in multiple systems, including in the Babylonian-Sumerian period, where there's sort of an original chaos goddess, Tiamat, and then she's killed, and then out of her body the raw material gets reorganized into what becomes the state. And so for an anarchist, it's still this concern with the state, but the state doesn't just mean government as opposed to corporations. The state is the way in which human beings kind of deny the underlying chaos, or Tao, that is always outside of our structures, our language, our cultural patterns, our institutions — and that there's something fundamentally valuable about returning, even for a moment, even in the space of a riot or the space of a sexual ritual or the space of a psychedelic trip, but more hopefully in a longer-term way, returning to that kind of primeval chaos as a kind of refreshing reminder that it doesn't lie in forms of human power. That's not the answer.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And so that anarchism for him is both political and spiritual and philosophical, because it takes the form of ontological anarchism. What does that mean? It means the fundamental questions about what is reality. You want to boil it down: what is reality? What's really real? How do we think about it? Do we think about it in terms of science? Do we think about it in terms of consciousness? Do we think about it in terms of history, like natural history, Darwinism, evolutionary forms? How do we think about it? And the ontological anarchism is like, the thing itself is multiple, or the thing itself is chaotic, is turbulent, is made of multiplicities. There is no there there that boils down to a single perspective or a single way of being. It's multiple perspectives all the way down. So when you have that attitude — and that's part of what is so transformative about Wilson, because we can call that a postmodern perspective.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's a metasystemic viewpoint.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Right. Yeah. And so we can talk about it with other terms, but in terms of popular thinking, that's kind of the word that ended up standing for the metasystem thinking, where you recognize there's a multiplicity of perspectives, and they kind of relate, but there's not a God's-eye view, although there are different hierarchies within that point of view. And that's a very revolutionary idea when you first encounter it. And in a lot of ways, within occultism and within psychedelics and so on in the underground, he was one of the first people to really, really push that perspective, really articulate it very strongly, so you couldn't fall back on simple ideas of truth. There's origins for it, it goes back, you can find it in Taoism, you can find it in Crowley, and it's not like he invented it all — but he articulated it in a way that blew your mind. Just the fact of the multiplicity, that there are these multiple reality tunnels and we're navigating between them all the time. Just communicating that reality was both liberating and vertiginous, kind of frightening.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Kind of, oh boy, oh, here we go — kind of like, what, I took how much LSD? Oh, look at the clock, here it comes. You know, there's an aspect of, like, you can't go back from that perspective very easily unless you rigorously hold on to something. You go, okay, all that multiple-perspective stuff is, yeah, it's true to a certain degree, but where we really root reality is in science, or rationality, or history, or structure, or whatever the thing is. But it becomes harder to do. And so I think that that's partly why Cosmic Trigger is potent, because it shows that philosophically, but it also shows what happens when that kind of viewpoint starts to be coupled with in-your-face experiences that grow farther and farther away from the norm. And you realize that you don't have an easy way back.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, he does it to you as the reader by presenting: well, I thought such-and-such was happening, but the real thing, I realized, was probably happening. And he builds this whole alternate narrative that you buy into, and then he crashes that one. Oh, that's not happening, it was something completely different. And he builds another one that you now buy into, and each one is just progressively weirder and more out there and more totally freakish. And you find yourself — now this is the last thing to hang on to — and then he crashes that one. And so you just get plunged into the depths of multi-perspectival thinking, and also watching yourself grab on and then having it pulled away, and grab on and having it pulled away. I think of it as not only a demonstration of metasystemic thinking, or postmodern thinking, but also it's just emptiness, right? It's just, here's nondual awareness for you. Like, let's play with how you get right into that by pulling away your conceptual maps over and over and over. I never saw him use that word, but I can't see any meaningful difference between the chaotic bones of Tiamat and what Wilson is saying and what Nagarjuna is talking about.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, no, I think that it is very much a via negativa. And it reminds me of something — this is just a slightly different direction, but something a friend of mine said not long ago, who was a philosopher. We were talking about philosophies of multiplicity, philosophies where you don't try to say that when you boil the world down you come to one thing, and where you're always insisting, no, there's always this kind of seething multiplicity that we may organize in patterns of unity, but the thing itself is multiple, is plural, is fundamentally plural. And he said that that pluralism — he was also a Buddhist — pluralism was a lot closer to nonduality than the one. And I think that's super profound.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it's why they call it in Sanskrit advaita, right? Not the word oneness, it's the word not-two-ness, right? So it's very interesting.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah. And I think that that's something that I find that a lot of, like, the sort of Bay Area esoteric, spiritual, meditative, Eastern, transpersonal, meta thing — that whole kind of rich current that you and I have played in the waters of for quite a while now, in different ways — one of the problems with it, like in the Science and Nonduality zone, is there's just way too much emphasis on unity in the form of the nondual, or how people are conceiving the nondual. But it's a lot of oneness, and not that much wrestling with real difference, like difference that hurts, or difference that does not go — like, how does that become an opportunity for either insight, or for demonstrating emptiness, or for being kind of initiated into a different way of seeing?

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: I mean, it's kind of just sort of a sidelight, but I still just think of that element of pluralism, of the multiple perspectives within the metasystemicity — and really not just saying, oh, it's multiple, but really wrestling with the fact that they don't quite fit, and having to relocate between them, and see what different perspectives say about other perspectives. It's an open-ended game. It's not always very fun to play, but I think it's a lot more insightful, particularly now, than a somewhat easy emphasis on a kind of gesture towards the nondual that's sort of like a gesture towards the one.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, sort of like a gesture towards God or some kind of God concept, right? It's really fascinating that someone like Ken Wilber — who, you know, interesting guy, I've hung out with him to a certain extent — his whole game is, let's make all those multiplicities fit together into one giant quilt that we kind of sew together. And that's it, that's the one move he's going to make: try to locate everything on this gigantic map and have it all fit somehow. I learned a lot from that move, but it doesn't actually work in the end. You just notice interesting connections. But there's whole places where these maps conflict in a way that cannot be resolved. And that's the good part, right? That's what's interesting, or gives you insights into something that you were assuming was a given or whatever. The move to just kind of hammer away all the differences in the service of making it one giant map doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah. Yeah. No, I agree.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And somehow Wilson got that from the get-go. I don't know how. It seems like something that people who take psychedelics seem to get more intuitively than people who don't. Maybe, you know, it's just my warped perception, I'm not sure, but...

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: No, I think there's something to be said for it. I mean, I think that one of the reasons to explore psychedelics that's beyond hedonism or pure curiosity is because I believe it helps — although it can also hinder along these lines — but it helps move and become comfortable with operating with multiple perspectives, and recognizing that that implies a kind of emptiness, or a kind of no ultimate position within it, and that that can be vertiginous, and you've got to kind of get used to it. And it's kind of scary. If you actually look at it straight on, it can be really scary, or really kind of bleak, or, oh my God, there's no answer, or whatever. There's a kind of existential moment in that, that comes out of being able to see these different perspectives. But it's sort of good training when you come back down, when you're not quite so blown out. I think it can lead — not necessarily, but it can lead — to more facility with moving around.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: But in Wilson's case, I think he had that sensibility sort of from the get-go, I think long before he started taking psychedelics. He took peyote for a spell in the early 60s and then didn't take LSD for a very long time. I mean, he met Leary and hung out. He wasn't like a super psychedelicized guy in the 60s. I mean, he was, but it wasn't like a central practice.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: He's more of a pothead.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, yeah, exactly. And maybe we might even be able to talk about that in terms of pot. I mean, pot is so ubiquitous today that it's kind of hard to theorize about, but I think it is the case — I talk about this a little in the forthcoming book — that pot has psychedelic effects, was definitely psychedelic for Wilson, for Terence McKenna. And one of the things it does is also kind of show multiple perspectives, multiple angles, different ways of looking at things.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: But in Wilson's case, it was also just encountering Korzybski and the idea that the map is not the territory, and that language, in a sense, stands in the way of reality. And once you have that perspective, which is also kind of shared with Zen or Taoism and other traditions — once you have that perspective, it's not that language is just an illusion, it's that it actually kind of constructs reality in different ways, but it's still relative. And once you really take that on, then you're always going to be interested in pointing, well, how do we get outside of language? And if we can't get outside of it, how do we at least deconstruct it sufficiently to open up something like that Tiamat chaos space again?

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And it makes you inherently suspicious about full-on reality claims, because they're in language, because they're another model, they're another map. So if I don't believe the map, if I don't believe language can ever really grok reality or capture reality, then I'm going to tend towards a certain kind of relativism, a certain kind of pluralism. Because I say, well, you could use that language game or this language game, and some of them are better than others, probably more likely to lead to useful results. But that kind of pragmatism in relationship to these multiple possibilities, to me, is the thing that he does. And I think part of what we respond to positively in Wilson is not just his blowing our minds with these multiple perspectives — and he's kind of a trickster, and he can be a little mean sometimes, and kind of a bullshitter.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Or a lot hilarious.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, hilarious. You know, he's kind of a bullshitter in some ways. But it's that he's also very pragmatic, meaning that, given this crazy situation we're in, what are the best results for the values that I have? Whether it's, you know, light and love, family, insight, entertainment, whatever it is — let's actually work with the things that we have. Let's not get ideological. Let's not get militant about any of our perspectives, even if we take them really seriously. And I think that offers some guidance through this labyrinth in a way that he introduces you to.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, after he left being an editor at Playboy, right, at some point he got a PhD in psychology. And he wrote that interesting book, actually — it's not just Cosmic Trigger, there's a lot of books by him I really like. I still would read The Illuminatus! Trilogy anytime, that's just too much fun. But he wrote that book called Quantum Psychology. And some of it is whatever, some of it's very suspect, pseudoscience as far as I'm concerned. But a whole bunch of that book is just exercises in taking other perspectives, exercises in switching the model you're using. There are exercises at the end of it to just force yourself to take new perspectives and practice doing that. And I have gone back to that book over and over again, because the exercises are really powerful. And even just reading it — even if you don't do the exercises, although he exhorts you over and over again, you know, don't just read this, you have to really do it — but even reading it, it's a fascinating book. And I see how he eventually formalized this idea, right, with his Korzybskian stuff, these sort of practices that he developed for this stuff. Not that he was ever explicitly a spiritual teacher or whatever.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: But that's that pragmatism, you know. And that leads to another interesting question. You just said, like, not that he was a spiritual teacher — and then you go, what is a spiritual teacher? What makes a spiritual teacher different from somebody who is handing you a lot of very useful techniques and practices? It's like, oh, it's kind of interesting. There is a difference. He wasn't a spiritual teacher, and yet it was very practical in some ways, even though it was blowing your mind. And here's quantum physics, and here's existentialism, and here's the history of the esoteric, and here's some conspiracy theory. I mean, it's this crazy world that he's presenting. And at the same time, there is a practical dimension to it, especially in that book and a few others, where he emphasizes specific practices that you can do that are going to change your mind and on some level change your brain.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Prometheus Rising, which is the other one.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, Prometheus Rising, which is one of my other favorites there. Yeah, in that way he's very... And also, again, prophetic, like you talked about. There's so much stuff that was sort of anticipated, where he kind of saw what we now think of as consciousness hacking, or kind of neural approaches to mysticism, in the context of a kind of tool-oriented pragmatism rather than a spiritual technique. Like, this is a spiritual technique handed down from masters centuries old, we use it with great reverence. He's like, no, it's a tool, it's a technique, it's this thing that'll help you realize how the brain works and give you a little more room, perhaps, to avoid the programs you don't want and to install the programs you do want, and to experience some more of the personal freedom that was his kind of main goal.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: He's interesting to contrast with — and that's one of the things I write about with all three of these figures. I got my PhD in religion, in religious studies, and I looked at modern religion, spirituality, New Age, modern occultism, modern esotericism.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You're like into California Christianity.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, that's something else. I've studied that quite a lot, actually. But what I really like about all these figures is the way that their work, and even their personas or their characters, gets close to something like religion or even spirituality — religion is probably a better term to use — and at the same time is not. You know, it's not. Even though there's like materials there, and here's the esoteric, and there's some Sufism, and then there's this Gnosticism, and all this stuff that's kind of like the material of religion — we could sit around and define religion for the next hour, but just to use back-of-the-envelope kind of language. And yet at the same time, there's a resistance to religion. There's a kind of secularity. There's a kind of freedom, a kind of democratic spirit of, like, let's just go and explore, or a kind of scientific...

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: He would always pop the bubble, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, you know, same thing with McKenna, where McKenna comes up with these crazy scenarios — you know, aliens moving in, and the history of alchemy is actually this, and da-da-da — but on another level he's like, look, go try it out: five grams in quiet darkness and you're good to go. You can be the explorer, don't listen to me. So that kind of willingness to not be the guru. Wilson had a lot of charisma. He definitely played the guru, he definitely played the kind of mischief-maker, Crowley-like figure in a way. But there was another side of that, which was very humble and goofy and, you know, cigarette-smoking and hanging out and not holding on to that kind of reverence.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And to me, that tension between a kind of psychedelic or mystical religiosity, with all of this esoterica and this kind of sense of possibility and enchantment and wonder on the one hand, and on the other hand a much more pragmatic kind of science-informed, skeptical side — I think that the sweet spot to be in, in the mysteries, in our own personal search, and in trying to figure out how our search fits in with the larger world, the sweet spot is between those. It's one foot in each world. And it's not that comfortable, and sometimes confusing. But to kind of fall on one side or the other too much, I think, is actually more of a delusion, frankly.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You know, what I see here in the Bay Area, especially in what we could call tech bro culture, but in the culture generally, are a lot of people who are very — what a few years ago we would have just called very nerdy, right? Very tech, STEM, mathematics kind of guys, wired kind of tight, who are really interested in psychedelics and really using them, really trying to learn meditation for real, going to raves, going to Burning Man, all this. And this is stuff that previously would have only been — it was marginalia to the nth degree, or if it wasn't, it was a completely different part of culture, right? It's like the high weirdness freaks, not these sort of rocket-scientist guys, except maybe for Jack Parsons. But I'm curious what you see going on there. Like, is this part of a current culture of awakening, or is this just the new way to kind of make yourself...

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: You know, I have really complex feelings about it. And I've been lately kind of reflecting — I'm in my 50s and I'm very much a creature of the worlds that shaped me, and I attempt to update myself to a certain degree. I now, like a lot of people as they age, realize that their cultural frameworks and cultural perspectives are kind of dwindling.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Archaic.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Archaic, yeah. You're like, oh wait, I'm a fossil — especially now, with all the change. And not just all the change, but the fact that younger generations... I think this is one of the key kind of sociological things to remember for those of us who are older and kind of wrestling with this issue: it's not just that technology is changing, or that we're ossifying, or can't keep up, or don't want to keep up, or whatever. But it's also that the younger generations came up in a technological environment that emphasized horizontality, that emphasized their connections with one another, and de-emphasized the more traditional vertical relationship between generations or between different statuses in society.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So even in our kind of post-counterculture zone, or post-baby-boom zone, where there was a lot of criticism of tradition, our experiences are still much more modeled on these kinds of connections through time. Who came before us? Who knows more than we do? And the new zone is way more horizontal. Everybody's out there kind of making their own thing, probing their own thing, sharing it with each other. And the people who came before — it's like, yeah, they can help with some things maybe, there's some people who are really interested, but a lot of people just aren't that interested in the experiences of a kind of different generation. So I recognize that I just don't really understand that world on some level, and that when I speak about it, and particularly when I critique it, it's partly from who I am.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So when I think about this tech bro turning on, microdosing, consciousness hacking, one thing to say about it is that it's extremely tool-oriented. And the thing about the tool as a metaphor — so it's like, psychedelics are a tool. And a lot of people say this, even psychotherapists and people in the underground who are working on psychedelics to work through problems will talk about them as tools, or medicines. But tools is really the more appropriate metaphor. But the thing about the tool is, the tool always implies a tool user who has intent.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So once you start talking about them as tools, even before you say what they're tools for, just by calling them tools you have also created the subject, the tool user, who uses them for certain purposes. And that's not necessarily the best way, or certainly not the only way, to enter into a relationship with psychedelics. There's a lot to be said for not having a clue what you're doing. There's also a fair amount to be said for going, this is a relationship with maybe not an entity, but something that has something to say, that I have to kind of learn what it means to be in relationship with. I think psychedelics are much more learning experiences than tool-using experiences. In a way, it's a pedagogical relationship, and that's different than a tool-using relationship.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So that's part of what I think the difference is when you say, is this part of a new form of awakening or a new grooviness? I think another possible way of saying it is, it's another example of how capitalism absorbs its edges. And I say that not thinking that I wasn't part of the same process. You can tell a story about the whole counterculture where, in a sense, what was happening — this isn't the whole truth, but it is a truth — in a sense what was happening was an immense liberation of desire and cultural possibility that created all of these experimental situations, some of which became very useful and were crystallized and absorbed into an expanding form of capitalism which reaches its tendrils ever more minutely into the core of your subjectivity. And that's kind of what we're at now.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So that's a dark kind of dystopian view: that now psychedelics are just part of the tool set. It's a new space and a new way for those logics to absorb the kind of creative energy that is produced through psychedelics.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Very large pharmaceutical companies who are taking people who have been psychedelic guides and sitters on the margins of society for the past 30 years, leading people through trips, you know, in the rainforest in British Columbia or whatever — and they actually brought them in and paid them and learned all their techniques, and now they're patenting all that. So it is getting just ultra-absorbed right into the core of the capitalist monster.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, so that's one way of talking about it. I think another way of thinking about psychedelics today in technology culture — the microdosing world is just one example of that. It's a very clear example of how, oh look, this compound that, if you take it in enough of a dose, will melt down all of your reality constructs and force you to face the glittering, goofy void of the cosmos, at a lower level can help your productivity, modulate your mood, enable you to maybe be a little more creative with the kind of work that you have to do. That's not an inherently bad thing, but it's certainly an example of how a potentially radical or even revolutionary compound can be whittled down into something that's a performance enhancer. And once it's a performance enhancer — you know, I like enhancing performance as much as anybody, but it is also part of the logic of contemporary capitalism, where we're all, as selves, as individuals doing our work, we're all kind of entrepreneurs of ourselves, and branding ourselves, and maximizing our potential, and just keeping the whole thing going. And in a way, that's also part of what's happening.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: But I think a third element is that knowledge and the ability to explore, manipulate, open up altered states of consciousness is now kind of on the table. It's like, oh, I could see it coming, I knew this was going to happen. This is one where I was, like, totally clear. As soon as you have a scientific focus on the brain, and that all reality is created by the brain — like mainstream materialism — and the idea that, oh, psychological problems, that doesn't have to do with your mom or some story and some Freudian thing, no, there's like a problem in the brain, we can work on it with these techniques and take an SSRI. So once we kind of move into a very biological, brain-based approach to psychological experience, or even to consciousness, you've got something set up there, which is that, well, at some point you're going to have to explain this other stuff that happens to brains sometimes.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Like, you know, whatever — synchronicities, out-of-body experiences, near-death experiences, and most obviously psychedelics. Because all those other ones, well, we're not sure what they mean, are they people's stories, and it's not going to hurt — but something definitely happens on a big dose of DMT. And if you're going to have a robust explanation for the brain and for the relationship of consciousness and the brain, even if you're not interested in psychedelics at all, you're going to have to come up with a really good story. But once you have to come up with a really good story about what's going on with the brain and psychedelics — oh, the cat's out of the bag. Oh, now psychedelics are on the table. Oh wait, what does it mean? Oh boy. Okay, what do we do with that?

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And I think a lot of what we're seeing now is — this is one story, I don't know if it's true — sometimes I think a lot of what we're seeing now is that people can't really deal with the full reckoning of what that means, because in their extreme, psychedelics are terrifying, scrabbling, exalting, and deeply, deeply weird. And I don't want to deal with — no, we don't want to deal with that. So, oh, they're good for that, they're good for PTSD, they're good for whatever. And not that those people are wrong, or that they're hiding something by emphasizing either the healing or the efficiency or the creativity or the usefulness — all of those things I think are true, or can be true. But I think it's partly the way that our society is kind of going, oh, there is this thing we haven't really come to terms with about the mind, about the nature of reality, about these compounds, and that we're really only just beginning to sort of see what happens when we engage with that. So it might just be a phase, if you will.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: But at the same time, I think you lose a very, very important tantric spark when these things are no longer illegal. You know, if you think of tantra — what does that mean? We could talk forever, another four hours, on tantra. But one core aspect of it is that you are dealing, in a ritual context, with things that are culturally forbidden. It's the totally secret, forbidden, loss-of-caste type stuff. And so that aspect shapes not just the meaning of drugs like psychedelics, which of course are still illegal, and so that's a more complicated one — but cannabis is very clear. Not just the meanings of it from afar: it's the actual kind of subjectivity, the engagement of it, the relationship with it, is modulated partly by its social condition.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So once you make it legal, it just changes the vibe. Whether or not it becomes hyper-commercialized or simply decriminalized or whatever, there's something that's changed. It's not bad, it's not good, but it is real. And the idea that my relationship to cannabis when I can go to jail for 10 years for a joint, versus when I can go to the corner store and buy an ounce of stronger weed — that that isn't different is, I think, kind of foolish. And so some of that is happening in psychedelics now, even if technically they're still illegal on the street, and that will remain that way for a very long time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Except maybe in Oregon.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, maybe. Yeah, it's true, you don't know. You know, it could be psilocybin. It could happen, it really could. But until then, we're still seeing big social stories changing around them, and that's going to have downstream effects even on the vibe that I think we're only beginning to tune into.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Something similar has happened with meditation, right? Probably this is impossible, but theoretically, if you had learned Buddhist meditation 500 years ago, they would have killed you in Europe for that, right? Like, okay, you're doing something completely non-Christian — although, of course, there were Christian forms of contemplative practice. But still, that would have been as illegal as it gets. And then you have people in the 20th century experimenting with it, and it's still pretty countercultural and weird and different. Then in the 90s, the Buddhist community in America went out of its way to kind of tame the whole thing and make it completely acceptable, and totally gelded it to the point where it's, you know, as safe as milk. And now we're microdosing mindfulness at work.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Part of my job is teaching people in corporations to meditate, so I believe in doing that. And yet at the same time, it does have this similar feature of being the kind of tamest possible version of something radically mind-expanding and reality-bending or -exploding. And you see people like Willoughby Britton, who are dealing with the edge of that, where people who take this safe little dose of meditation every day go just a little too far with it, in quotes, and they start having really intense experiences, and that's not what they signed up for. And so there's always been this parallelism, I think, between psychedelics and meditation. Certainly in America, they go together hand in hand.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And it's funny that both of them are being introduced now, or have been introduced, as performance-enhancing brain hacks that are going to help you as a worker drone be kind of special. And there's something really, in a way, cool about that. And in another way, it's like, huh, what happened to the tantric spark, as you put it? What happened to the thing that caused me to go to India and sit underground for months, you know, to learn this stuff, with centipedes crawling the walls and no food and stuff? It's like, there was a thing there that was so captivating and beautiful and just amazingly expansive and, in a way, not forbidden, but certainly weird, that just isn't even part of the conversation right now.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Part of where I've kind of wound up — I mean, I never really intended, when I started writing and being a cultural critic and writing about the history of technology and writing a lot about music, I didn't think that I would wind up spending so much of my time thinking and talking about psychedelics. And one of the reasons I do, and one of the reasons I wrote the book that I did, is that I think one of the important things for at least people like me to do now within that domain — and also within Buddhism, that's a separate conversation, but I feel a similar devotion towards certain aspects of Buddhism, although I've written much less about it — is just emphasizing keeping it weird, or reminding everyone that the weird is in the room now.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And they may get caught up in this thing about psychology, and fixing this, and the new accreditation system, and pharmacies, and blah blah blah. There's so much other stuff for people to go to as it becomes mainstream. And I'm just kind of like, yeah — and if you take enough, it's really weird. That's all I can say. I don't have to say it's spiritual, I don't have to say it's sacred, I don't have to say it gives you truth. I don't know. I mean, I have my opinions, that's a separate conversation. But what I am saying is, it's weird. And the weird is real. The weird is part of reality. It's not a distortion of what is otherwise seen with clarity. Weirdness, anomaly, not knowing where you are, confusion, a vague sense of wondrous unease — those things are stitched, I believe, into the nature of this game that we're in, and psychedelics are going to open up that space, at least for some of us.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And the way I think about it now — before, you were alluding to this group Compass, which is a for-profit pharmaceutical-based form of a company that, after acting like it was a nonprofit and being really groovy and talking to a lot of researchers who were really open-minded, hoovered all their information and is now kind of shelled up, and is trying to establish a kind of — I don't want to say monopoly, but at least control over a network of therapy centers, mostly in Europe, where they're going to be producing psilocybin through a trademarked way, or a patentable way of producing a synthetic psilocybin, and using them inside clinics that they run and control. So it's obviously a huge pyramid, whatever — it's a whole vertically integrated corporation where there's potential to make a lot of money. And meanwhile, other people are saying, hey, we can do a nonprofit form where we're just making things available at cost and blah blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: But there's another outside to all this. Even as it develops and people look at it and focus on it, there's still all these mushrooms growing up in the grass. And as long as there's a culture of bored teenagers going crazy, and people who commune with nature, and people who like weird experiences, there's going to be this zone that's outside of it. And people who are taking these things as ways of insight into plant consciousness, or ways of insight into the nature of reality, or as portals or rocket ships that'll blast you into other kinds of dimensions. You continue to cultivate that space, because it will never be strictly controlled. That's what's kind of amazing about it. Because even if they control it, it's not any different than prohibition. There's still going to be those outsides. We don't think about them, we don't talk about them, because it's all about this mainstreaming effort. But it's just nice to remember that the mushrooms are still growing between the blades of the grass.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it's interesting to me that — again, I'll go back to this parallelism with the meditation. I'm curious if you see some similar property there, that no matter how corporate it may become, we can still do our own practice at home, or perhaps go to some other cultural context and learn weird practices, or something that maintains that edge of danger and forbiddenness and possibility, right? Real power.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: I think about it personally maybe a little bit less in terms of the weird or the exotic, and a little bit more in terms of, frankly, the religious. And I mean that in a good sense. So one way of saying the kind of problem is Buddhism when it hits the West.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: What's your relationship with Buddhist practice?

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: I started studying Madhyamaka, you know, Gelugpa, Tibetan Buddhism, in the early 90s. I didn't love the structured lamrim-style meditation practices. I was like, that was not my style. So I started looking for meditation places, and I found a Zen group in New York City, Manhattan, and they were part of the Maezumi Roshi lineage, which kind of combines Soto and Rinzai approaches. And I just started sitting then. And I went through many years of being very much a capital-Z Zen practitioner: lots of sesshin, lots of sitting, and reading.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: By the early 2000s, I was kind of both not so happy in my practice situation, but also increasingly alienated and even a little sickened by the discourse of American Buddhism. So I kind of checked out. I kept sitting. I've always been pretty much a shikantaza, just-sit, breath-work person, but not a lot of visualization or really complex meditations. I've done a little bit of that stuff, I like it, but my core sitting is kind of the shikantaza-Dzogchen line. And I've never been a disciplined twice-daily sitter. I've always been sloppy, and I felt bad about it forever, for years. And then finally, one day I was like, oh wait, somehow along the way I still kind of became a mature practitioner, even though I'm not really following the rules. So I have a pretty idiosyncratic approach, which I'm really quite happy about, especially now that I'm doing a little bit more formal practice again. It's like, I have this whole body of independent ways of thinking and doing these things that I'm very appreciative for.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So I have a great respect for meditation, both for its sort of psychologically curative effects, but more just for its interest. What a marvelous microscope we've been given, or set of exploratory tools, to be able to go into these realms. And they're right. I mean, I remember Maezumi Roshi saying back in the 90s, he was like, you just keep doing this — he didn't say "get to my age," but that was the implication — you get older, you've just got this like yummy pot cooking in your belly all the time. And it's true. It's a great relief and a literal joy, the fruits of meditation after doing it for a long time. I mean, it's not just cognitive and psychological effects. You generate bliss states in your body that can stabilize you and keep you from getting caught up with all the glittery lights of the desire world as mediated through postmodern capitalism. You're like, yeah, I could do that, or I could just sit down for 10 minutes and I'm feeling pretty good. You know, that's nice. I don't need anybody else.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: I mean, it's an amazing thing to existentially realize in the core of your own experience that, in some ways — it's not an absolute statement, but in some ways — I can make myself happy. Or, "happy" isn't even the right word — just bliss, or intimacy, presence. It's right there. It's right there. So I love that stuff. And I'm happy that middle-manager sports fans in Iowa are given the opportunity to introduce something like this into their lives.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Me too, yeah. I think that's a good thing.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So then it becomes this question of, how do you encourage the highest percentage of those people who are doing that kind of mainstream meditation to enter into the deeper folds of it? And this is where, again, the religious aspect becomes kind of interesting. So go back — you think, like, okay, Buddhism's coming in. It's a mix, in a way, to use modern terminology, where there's this religion over here, and there's science over there, and there's psychology kind of on the science side but overlapping a little bit, helping explain religion. And you get this Buddhist package, and whether you're talking Tibetan Buddhism, where it's really obvious — Zen is a little more sneaky about it, Theravada even a little bit more sneaky about it — it's this combination of religion and what we would think of as kind of secular, scientific, psychological, secular.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And that mixture was always there. You know, like, some people were really believing these tantric deities were in the room, and they're becoming them, and there's this whole magical universe that they're interacting with, powerful objects and chants that are based on the holy guru from the past, all that kind of stuff, which, whatever the details, looks and smells like religion — because it's kind of religion. And at the same time, there are these principles and practices — not just the practices, but actually the kind of mind principles that you can distill from them — that clearly resemble and work very well within a secular context, that we can psychologize. We can think about them in terms of how the brain works. We can think about them in terms of how the mind works. And over the last few decades, that side of it, the secular side of it, has become more and more potent, more and more dominant.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And that was part of that 90s move of, like, let's defang this as much as possible. Let's de-counterculturalize Buddhism as much as possible. So they turned to psychology and they turned to neuroscience. Those are the main ones.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And medicine.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And medicine, right. And putting it in a medical kind of context. So in a way, the problem of corporate mindfulness is an inevitable outcome of that. Because now that we've defanged it enough, we've made it secular enough, that even mainstream corporations — who don't want to have anything to do with weird New Age stuff or whatever — even it becomes thinkable in those environments, and for people who are working in those environments.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So in a way, we need to balance that. It's, in a sense, a return to religion. Not a return to religion in the boring sense of, oh, you've got to do the rituals, or we start believing in the hierarchy again, but more in the core motivations, which are liberation, the fact that the world is suffering, the fact that you're going to die, that it's going to suck, probably, that everybody you know is going to die, that everything's going away. And those kinds of questions don't fit too well in the boardroom. You don't have to be religious about them, but they're kind of religious questions. So they're the kind of questions that religious people ask, are obsessed with, try to work through, and believe that you can work through, rather than just going, oh, there's no meaning, give up, don't worry, just enjoy life while you have it, and then you're going to die and be in the ground and it doesn't matter — instead of nihilism.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So if you're not going to be nihilist about those things, then in some ways you're picking up this sort of religious seeking. And it's less about making sure that meditation is wild and wacky. It's almost more about making sure that it remains coupled to these insights and these questions, so that at least some of the people who are exposed to corporate mindfulness will begin to go, wait, this job is kind of meaningless, or, you know, I'm going to die — do I want this to be what I do until I die? Or, gosh, you know, that product we're making, that we make in China, it's actually full of toxics, oh, I don't know if I could... you know, whatever those kinds of questions are, whatever kinds of world-activating, value-shifting insights are, they're coupled implicitly with these practices.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: I don't know how you maintain it, whether you just make sure you keep the conversation robust alongside the corporate mindfulness, so at least you draw some people over, whether you become kind of a foot soldier and you go into those realms with these deeper questions intact. I mean, how do you do it? Like, when you're teaching these things and you can see, maybe even with certain individuals, like, well, this person's really going down there, okay, they might be ready for something a little more heavy than — that is beyond my purview as a corporate mindfulness teacher. So, I mean, I'm curious, how do you balance those?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, we do see that, not often, but often enough. You see someone who's having either a major experience right there in the middle of your day-long retreat at a corporation, or who reports that doing the practices at home, even 10 minutes a day, is starting to really have some strange and interesting and sometimes disturbing effects. Obviously, sometimes the correct way of dealing with it, as far as I'm concerned, is to tell them to slow down or back off a little bit, because it's so destabilizing and their personal goals seem to be really about stability.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But for people who seem to be, let's say, robust, or a little bit into the instability, who are eager to go after those questions, then there's the local center, the local meditation center. And I wouldn't necessarily recommend mine over somebody else's or whatever, but I'll see what they're into and see if they have openness to going and sitting at a day-long, a little bit more, let's say, hardcore meditation retreat, or beginning to read that material — and even in a very non-Buddhist kind of way begin to expose them to that realm of ideas. You may be aware that down in the Mission we've got the San Francisco Dharma Collective now, in the past month or two.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So what was previously Against the Stream — when that collapsed, I was a teacher there. The students, all of whom are really interesting countercultural figures, at least many of whom are, were like, yeah, screw this, we're not going to let our center go away just because the teacher messed up. So they basically took over and created a new entity called the San Francisco Dharma Collective that is — you were talking about the horizontality — it's student-led, community-based, there is no root teacher, and they're running it. So something like that, where it's very vibrant: the sense of vibrancy and aliveness and interest and energy skyrocketed immediately as soon as they took it over. The engagement level is just awesome to see. But that's the kind of place where I might go, yeah, you might want to go down there and just sit in on some meditations and see what's going on, because you're not going to get indoctrinated into someone's religion or someone's particular guru-hood or whatever. It's a little safer than that.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Yeah, I mean, I think that's the tricky spot. It's, again, one of these one-foot-in-both-worlds, or balancing along the line, that there's something — even though there's so much in traditional religion that's wrong, and we can see the way that the guru model and inherited hierarchies and supernatural thinking and a lot of those things largely obscure a lot of the things that we want. They're valuable, they're interesting, there's reasons that maybe at some point in someone's life they plunge into more of a deeply religious practice. But there's something that's lost when we completely let all that go and just embrace secular values and, like, oh, these are things, we're going to explore them, they're going to help us do this, and we're going to deal with my psychology, deal with my obsessions, da-da-da-da. There's something that's lost in that, that leads towards the lack of dynamics in a kind of corporate situation.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So it's in a way a very narrow path, which again, in a psychedelic way, brings us back to some of the things I was saying about Terence and Robert Anton Wilson, where there's a navigating that's going on, the sense that part of what we want is — there's something within religion, there's some strands, there's some key motifs, that we want to be engaged with in the context of our still largely secular lives, to the point that maybe that distinction even begins to break down somewhat. And all of that's coming down the pike. It's like, the younger generation, the millennials — a quarter of them are like, no religion. I mean, it's changing radically.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: And so there's some kind of spiritual-but-not-religious sensibility that is kind of the future, but I think it's important to try to make sure it's still intense in some way. It's not just kind of easy, or whatever makes you feel good. There's still some kind of intensity, some kind of drive, some kind of confrontation with fear, confrontation with difficulty, confrontation with pain, embracing the shadow. That's more available when you open up beyond a purely secular framework, because within the secular framework it's about happiness and manifesting your goals, becoming more efficient, whatever. It tends to have this sort of positivity, happiness-seeking, to the point of denying any difficulties.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. And suffering.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: So what's going to draw you into suffering other than actual suffering you can't get away from, like disease or the loss of somebody? But it's there all the time. And I'm very much on that side, that it's about finding your light, whatever light you can gather, and stepping into that stuff. Whatever's going to help encourage that kind of process is very helpful.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Erik, thanks for coming on the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Erik Davis
transcript.text: Absolutely. I had a great time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's it for this episode of Deconstructing Yourself.
